query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, incorporating a reactive element X (Si, Mn, or Al) promotes the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent, slow-growing oxide layer above 900 °C by enabling preferential segregation of X at the metal/oxide interface. This segregation, enabled by the high configurational entropy of the alloy, reduces interfacial energy mismatches and moderates diffusion, thereby suppressing defect formation that would otherwise lead to cracking or spallation. In contrast, alloys without the appropriate X addition (or with insufficient X content) fail to develop such a protective scale under the same conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Homogeneously mixed single-phase high-entropy alloy (CrFeCoNiX) in a metallic solid-solution state, with X being Si, Mn, or Al.
generation.intervention: Exposing the alloy to an oxidative (or corrosive) atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (>900 °C) in a controlled oxidative environment with defined oxygen partial pressure and temperature ramp rates, ensuring a constant service environment.
generation.structural_mediator: Preferential segregation of the reactive element X to the metal/oxide interface facilitates the formation of a coherent, adherent oxide layer with reduced lattice mismatch.
generation.mechanism: High configurational entropy in the alloy enhances the uniform distribution of X; during high-temperature oxidation, X segregates to the surface where it reacts to form a slow-growing, stable oxide phase that minimizes defect formation (such as cracks or spalls) by reducing local strain and interfacial energy. This contrasts with alloys that lack sufficient X or have less effective segregation, which develop unstable oxides prone to spallation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys containing the optimal content of reactive element X (especially when X is chosen to balance reactivity and segregation behavior) will exhibit a slow-growing, continuous, and coherent protective oxide layer under high-temperature oxidative conditions, while baseline alloys lacking X or with a non-optimal X concentration will form unstable, cracked, or spalled oxide scales.
generation.baseline: A comparable CrFeCoNi alloy without the reactive element X serves as the control baseline.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is valid for high-entropy alloys in a single-phase metallic solution state, at temperatures above 900 °C, in oxidative/corrosive atmospheres typical of high-temperature service conditions. It is also delimited to compositions where the reactive element X is present in a concentration sufficient to promote segregation without compromising the single-phase structure.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the precise role and optimal concentration of each reactive element (Si, Mn, or Al) in promoting protective oxide layer formation and the potential influence of multiphase microstructures. Further experimental quantification is needed to determine the relative importance of segregation dynamics versus intrinsic oxidation kinetics in these alloys.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy alloys: one set of CrFeCoNi alloys without the reactive element X (baseline) and another set containing a defined amount of X (Si, Mn, or Al). Subject both sets to high-temperature oxidation tests above 900 °C in a controlled oxidative atmosphere. Conduct surface analyses (such as SEM, TEM, and XRD) after various time intervals to assess the oxide layer thickness, continuity, coating adherence, and incidence of spallation.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and growth rate (using cross-sectional microscopy)
Phase composition of the oxide scale (using XRD or XPS)
Occurrence and frequency of cracking or spallation events (through in-situ or ex-situ imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis would be falsified if the reactive-element-containing alloys fail to form a continuous and coherent protective oxide layer (i.e., they exhibit similar or increased rates of cracking/spallation compared to the baseline alloy) under the same exposure conditions, or if the baseline alloy without X forms a protective oxide layer at a rate and coherence comparable to that of the X-containing alloy.

cited_evidence.text:
Entropy-stabilized oxides

Abstract: Configurational disorder can be compositionally engineered into mixed oxide by populating a single sublattice with many distinct cations. The formulations promote novel and entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter where metal cations are incorporated in new ways. Here, through rigorous experiments, a simple thermodynamic model, and a five-component oxide formulation, we demonstrate beyond reasonable doubt that entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state. In the latter, cation distributions are proven to be random and homogeneous. The findings validate the hypothesis that deliberate configurational disorder provides an orthogonal strategy to imagine and discover new phases of crystalline matter and untapped opportunities for property engineering. The composition of oxide compounds controls many of their properties and electronic phases. Here, the authors show that entropy and configurational disorder can stabilize new phases of oxides, potentially enabling a better engineering of their properties.
